claim: Confidential assessment of Lovelace's mathematical ability: De Morgan says her 'power of thinking' on advanced mathematics was exceptional for a beginner of either sex, and that an equally promising young man headed to Cambridge would be prophesied to become 'an original mathematical investigator, perhaps of first rate eminence.'

claim: Re-dating key De Morgan-Lovelace letters from 1842 to 1840 overturns Dorothy Stein's reading that Lovelace was still struggling with functional equations two years into her studies; the authors conclude she had a solid grounding and might have reached research level with one or two more years.

claim: Clarifies the authorship debate: Babbage, not Lovelace, wrote the Analytical Engine's earliest programs (1836-37, in his notebooks, mostly unpublished and simpler than the Bernoulli-numbers table); documents a translation slip (French 'le cas de n=∞' rendered as 'the cos n=∞') and a bug in Operation 21 of her Bernoulli program; notes Howard Aiken (Harvard Mark I, 1944) built on Babbage's ideas without knowing of Lovelace's Notes, and that B.V. Bowden's 1953 'Faster Than Thought' first revived her reputation, calling her a 'prophet.'
